subject: ESS HL
question: Evaluate strategies for meeting demand for critical mineral resources while minimizing biodiversity loss, water pollution and social conflict.

rubricGroups.title: Analysis / systems / HL-lens connections
rubricGroups.titleJa: 分析・システム・HL lensとの接続

rubricGroups.title: Evaluation / perspectives / trade-offs
rubricGroups.titleJa: 評価・視点・トレードオフ

markscheme: Accurately explains critical minerals as finite mineral resources whose strategic importance and supply constraints can create resource-security concerns.
Accurately uses concepts such as non-renewable resource, resource stock, resource scarcity, resource security or resource depletion.
Accurately explains how mining can cause habitat loss, habitat fragmentation, pollution or changes to water systems.
Uses relevant sustainability concepts such as natural capital, ecosystem services, life-cycle impacts, restoration or circularity accurately.
Applies at least one strategy to reduce demand for virgin minerals, such as product longevity, material efficiency, reuse, recycling or substitution.
Applies at least one strategy to reduce impacts at extraction sites, such as careful site selection, pollution controls, tailings management, rehabilitation or biodiversity offsets where appropriate.
Applies at least one governance strategy, such as environmental-impact assessment, permitting, monitoring, rehabilitation bonds, community consultation or transparent supply-chain standards.
Uses a relevant real or clearly hypothetical mineral-extraction example to show how impacts depend on ore location, mining method, water availability, biodiversity and local communities.
Analyses how rising demand can increase extraction pressure and push mining into lower-grade ores, remote habitats or water-stressed regions.
Analyses how land clearance, roads and infrastructure can fragment habitats and create indirect pressures beyond the mine footprint.
Analyses how acid drainage, sediment, metals or processing wastes can affect water quality, aquatic ecosystems and downstream users.
Explains how recycling and circular material flows can reduce primary extraction but cannot immediately eliminate mining because demand growth, losses and stock turnover remain important.
Evaluates the environmental benefits and limitations of recycling, including collection rates, contamination, energy use and technological constraints.
Evaluates mine-site mitigation and restoration, recognizing that some biodiversity losses, hydrological changes or toxic contamination may be difficult to reverse fully.
Evaluates trade-offs between mineral supply for technologies and infrastructure versus local ecological damage, water use, livelihoods or cultural values.
Evaluates distributional and procedural justice, including who receives economic benefits, who bears environmental costs and whether affected communities participate meaningfully.
Develops an integrated strategy combining demand reduction, circularity, strict site-level safeguards, restoration and responsible sourcing rather than relying on one measure.
Explains conditions for success such as credible monitoring, enforceable standards, transparent supply chains, financial responsibility for cleanup and community participation.
Recognizes that critical-mineral demand is context dependent and that substitution, recycling and extraction must be judged across the full life cycle rather than at one site only.
Reaches a clear, justified judgement about which combination of strategies can meet mineral demand while minimizing biodiversity, water and social impacts.
markschemeJa: critical mineralをstrategic importanceとsupply constraintによりresource-security concernを生み得るfinite mineral resourceとして正確に説明する。
non-renewable resource、resource stock、resource scarcity、resource security、resource depletionなどを正確に使う。
miningがhabitat loss、fragmentation、pollution、water-system changeを起こし得ることを正確に説明する。
natural capital、ecosystem services、life-cycle impact、restoration、circularityなどsustainability概念を正確に使う。
product longevity、material efficiency、reuse、recycling、substitutionなどvirgin mineral需要を減らすstrategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
site selection、pollution control、tailings management、rehabilitation、必要に応じbiodiversity offsetなどmine-site impact削減策を適用する。
EIA、permit、monitoring、rehabilitation bond、community consultation、transparent supply-chain standardなどgovernance strategyを適用する。
実例または明確なhypothetical mineral-extraction exampleでimpactがore location、mining method、water availability、biodiversity、local communityに依存すると示す。
demand増加がextraction pressureを高め、lower-grade ore、remote habitat、water-stressed regionへminingを広げ得ることを分析する。
land clearance、road、infrastructureがmine footprint外にもhabitat fragmentationとindirect pressureを生むことを分析する。
acid drainage、sediment、metal、processing wasteがwater quality、aquatic ecosystem、downstream userへ影響することを分析する。
recycling/circular flowはprimary extractionを減らせるが、demand growth、material loss、stock turnoverのためminingを直ちに不要にはできないと説明する。
collection rate、contamination、energy use、technology constraintを含めrecyclingのenvironmental benefitと限界を評価する。
一部biodiversity loss、hydrological change、toxic contaminationは完全回復が難しいことを認識しmine-site mitigation/restorationを評価する。
technology/infrastructureのmineral supplyとlocal ecological damage、water use、livelihood、cultural value間のtrade-offを評価する。
economic benefitとenvironmental costの分配、affected communityのmeaningful participationなどdistributional/procedural justiceを評価する。
demand reduction、circularity、strict site safeguard、restoration、responsible sourcingを組み合わせたintegrated strategyを構築する。
credible monitoring、enforceable standard、transparent supply chain、cleanupへのfinancial responsibility、community participationなど成功条件を説明する。
critical-mineral demandはcontext dependentであり、substitution、recycling、extractionをsingle siteではなくfull life cycleで評価すべきと認識する。
biodiversity・water・social impactを最小化しながらmineral demandを満たすstrategy combinationについて明確で根拠あるjudgementを示す。
modelAnswer: Demand for critical minerals can support low-carbon technologies and infrastructure, but expanding extraction can damage habitats, pollute water and create conflict with local communities. The first strategy should be to reduce unnecessary primary demand through longer product life, efficient design, reuse, recycling and substitution. These measures can lower pressure on virgin resource stocks, although rapid demand growth means mining will still be required. At extraction sites, strong environmental assessment, careful siting, tailings controls, water treatment, progressive rehabilitation and enforceable cleanup liability can reduce impacts. However, restoration cannot always replace intact ecosystems, and pollution such as acid drainage may persist for decades. Governance is therefore crucial: transparent supply chains, independent monitoring and meaningful community participation can improve accountability and reduce unequal distribution of costs. Overall, the strongest approach combines circular material use with strict environmental and social safeguards for unavoidable extraction. Meeting mineral demand is possible with lower impact, but only if policies address the whole life cycle and accept that some ecologically sensitive sites should not be mined.
modelAnswerJa: critical mineral需要はlow-carbon technologyやinfrastructureを支えますが、extraction拡大はhabitat damage、water pollution、local communityとのconflictを生み得ます。まずproduct life延長、efficient design、reuse、recycling、substitutionによってprimary demandを下げるべきです。ただし急速なdemand growthがあるためminingを完全にはなくせません。mine siteではEIA、careful siting、tailings control、water treatment、progressive rehabilitation、cleanup liabilityを組み合わせることでimpactを下げられます。一方、intact ecosystemをrestorationで完全に置き換えることはできず、acid drainageなどは長期化する可能性があります。transparent supply chain、independent monitoring、meaningful community participationも重要です。したがってcircular material useとavoidableでないextractionへの厳格なenvironmental/social safeguardを組み合わせ、full life cycleで管理することが最も有効です。

subject: ESS HL
question: Evaluate the extent to which measures that include natural capital and environmental costs provide a better guide to sustainable progress than GDP alone.

rubricGroups.title: Analysis / systems / HL-lens connections
rubricGroups.titleJa: 分析・システム・HL lensとの接続

rubricGroups.title: Evaluation / perspectives / trade-offs
rubricGroups.titleJa: 評価・視点・トレードオフ

markscheme: Accurately explains GDP as the monetary value of final goods and services produced within an economy and recognizes that it is not a direct measure of sustainability or well-being.
Accurately explains natural capital and natural income and why depletion of natural assets can reduce future ecosystem-service flows.
Accurately explains at least one adjusted indicator such as Green GDP, genuine progress indicator or natural capital accounting.
Uses relevant environmental-economics terminology such as externality, economic valuation, ecosystem-service valuation, public good or ecological economics accurately.
Applies an example in which conventional GDP can rise while pollution, habitat loss or resource depletion also increases.
Applies natural capital accounting or ecosystem-service valuation to a relevant environmental asset such as forests, wetlands, soils, fisheries or water systems.
Applies an alternative progress framework such as Green GDP, GPI or doughnut economics and explains what additional information it attempts to capture.
Uses a relevant real or clearly hypothetical national or regional context to show why indicator choice can affect policy priorities.
Analyses how GDP may count market activity generated by extraction or pollution cleanup without subtracting the loss of natural capital that caused the problem.
Analyses how environmental externalities and non-market ecosystem services can be omitted from ordinary market prices and national accounts.
Explains how natural capital accounting can reveal changes in stocks that may be hidden when decision-makers focus only on annual economic flows.
Connects ecological economics to the idea that economic activity is embedded within biophysical systems and constrained by ecological limits.
Evaluates the practical strengths of adjusted indicators for making environmental trade-offs more visible to governments, investors or the public.
Evaluates limitations of monetary valuation, including uncertainty, non-market values, cultural or intrinsic values and the difficulty of pricing irreversible ecological loss.
Evaluates comparability and data limitations, recognizing that complex indicators may depend on contested assumptions and may be harder to communicate than GDP.
Evaluates whether combining multiple social and ecological indicators may be preferable to replacing GDP with one alternative single number.
Develops an integrated argument that distinguishes economic output from sustainable progress and long-term well-being.
Explains conditions for useful indicator systems such as transparent methods, consistent data, ecological thresholds and regular reporting of both stocks and flows.
Recognizes that better measurement does not automatically produce better policy if political incentives, institutions or distributional conflicts remain unchanged.
Reaches a clear, justified judgement about the extent to which natural-capital and environmental-cost measures provide a better guide to sustainable progress than GDP alone.
markschemeJa: GDPをeconomy内で生産されたfinal goods/servicesのmonetary valueとして正確に説明し、sustainabilityやwell-beingの直接指標ではないと認識する。
natural capitalとnatural incomeを正確に説明し、natural assetのdepletionがfuture ecosystem-service flowを低下させ得ると示す。
Green GDP、GPI、natural capital accountingなど少なくとも1つのadjusted indicatorを正確に説明する。
externality、economic valuation、ecosystem-service valuation、public good、ecological economicsなどを正確に使う。
conventional GDPが増える一方でpollution、habitat loss、resource depletionも増える例を適用する。
forest、wetland、soil、fishery、water systemなどへnatural capital accounting/ecosystem-service valuationを適用する。
Green GDP、GPI、doughnut economics等を適用し、追加で何を捉えようとするか説明する。
実例または明確なhypothetical national/regional contextでindicator choiceがpolicy priorityを変え得ると示す。
GDPはextractionやpollution cleanupによるmarket activityを加算しても、その原因となったnatural capital lossを差し引かない場合があると分析する。
environmental externalityやnon-market ecosystem serviceがordinary market price/national accountから抜け落ちることを分析する。
natural capital accountingがannual economic flowだけでは隠れるstock changeを可視化できることを説明する。
ecological economicsをeconomyがbiophysical system内にembeddedされecological limitの制約を受ける考え方へ結びつける。
adjusted indicatorがenvironmental trade-offをgovernment、investor、publicに見えやすくする実用的な強みを評価する。
uncertainty、non-market value、cultural/intrinsic value、irreversible ecological lossのpricing difficultyなどmonetary valuationの限界を評価する。
complex indicatorはassumptionに依存しGDPより比較・communicationが難しい場合があるというdata/comparability limitationを評価する。
GDPを別のsingle numberに置き換えるよりsocial/ecological indicatorを複数組み合わせる方がよい場合を評価する。
economic outputとsustainable progress・long-term well-beingを区別するintegrated argumentを構築する。
transparent method、consistent data、ecological threshold、stock/flowのregular reportingなど有用なindicator systemの条件を説明する。
measurement改善だけではpolitical incentive、institution、distributional conflictが変わらなければbetter policyを保証しないと認識する。
natural capital/environmental costを含むmeasureがGDP aloneよりどの程度sustainable progressのよいguideとなるか明確で根拠あるjudgementを示す。
modelAnswer: GDP is useful for measuring market production, but it is a poor standalone guide to sustainability because it does not show whether economic activity is depleting the natural capital on which future well-being depends. Timber extraction, for example, can add to GDP while reducing forest carbon storage, biodiversity and water regulation. Pollution cleanup can also create measured economic activity after environmental damage has already occurred. Green GDP, genuine progress indicators and natural capital accounting attempt to correct this by recording environmental costs, social outcomes or changes in natural-asset stocks. Ecosystem-service valuation can make otherwise invisible benefits more visible in decisions. However, adjusted measures have limitations. Monetary values for biodiversity, cultural meaning or irreversible loss are uncertain and contested, and complex indicators may be difficult to compare. Overall, measures incorporating natural capital and environmental costs provide a substantially better guide than GDP alone, but no single indicator is sufficient. The strongest approach uses GDP alongside transparent ecological and social indicators, including explicit thresholds that monetary valuation should not override.
modelAnswerJa: GDPはmarket productionを測るには有用ですが、future well-beingを支えるnatural capitalが減っているかを示さないためsustainabilityのstandalone guideとしては不十分です。例えばtimber extractionはGDPを増やしてもforest carbon storage、biodiversity、water regulationを低下させる可能性があります。Green GDP、GPI、natural capital accountingはenvironmental cost、social outcome、natural-asset stockの変化を記録し、この欠点を補おうとします。ecosystem-service valuationも見えにくいbenefitをdecisionへ反映できます。ただしbiodiversity、cultural meaning、irreversible lossをmoneyで評価することにはuncertaintyとethical limitationがあります。したがってnatural capital/environmental costを含むmeasureはGDP aloneより優れますが、1つのindicatorで置き換えるよりGDPと複数のecological/social indicator、さらにecological thresholdを併用する方法が最も適切です。

subject: ESS HL
question: Discuss how environmental justice and contrasting ethical frameworks should influence decisions that distribute environmental benefits and risks among communities and generations.

rubricGroups.title: Analysis / systems / HL-lens connections
rubricGroups.titleJa: 分析・システム・HL lensとの接続

rubricGroups.title: Evaluation / perspectives / trade-offs
rubricGroups.titleJa: 評価・視点・トレードオフ

markscheme: Accurately explains environmental justice as fair distribution of environmental benefits and burdens together with meaningful participation in decisions.
Accurately explains intergenerational justice and recognizes obligations toward people who will experience future environmental consequences.
Accurately distinguishes at least two ethical frameworks or positions, such as utilitarianism, rights-based ethics, deontology, anthropocentrism, biocentrism or ecocentrism.
Uses relevant ethical terminology such as intrinsic value, instrumental value, moral standing, stewardship, moral responsibility or ethical dilemma accurately.
Applies environmental-justice reasoning to a concrete decision such as siting a mine, landfill, industrial facility, transport corridor, dam or protected area.
Applies at least one ethical framework to the same decision and shows how it can support a different conclusion or priority.
Applies intergenerational reasoning to resource depletion, pollution, climate risk or long-lived environmental damage.
Uses a relevant real or clearly hypothetical example to show how environmental benefits and burdens can be distributed unevenly across income groups, locations or generations.
Analyses how a policy that maximizes aggregate benefits can still create environmental injustice if costs are concentrated on a vulnerable group.
Analyses how rights-based or deontological reasoning can place limits on actions even when a cost-benefit calculation suggests net social benefits.
Explains how biocentric or ecocentric reasoning can extend moral concern beyond direct human welfare to organisms, species or ecosystem integrity.
Explains how participation, recognition and access to decision-making can affect legitimacy, trust and distributional outcomes.
Evaluates utilitarian or consequentialist approaches by considering their ability to compare total benefits and harms alongside the risk of sacrificing minorities for aggregate gain.
Evaluates rights-based approaches by considering protection from serious harm alongside conflicts between competing rights or practical constraints.
Evaluates anthropocentric, biocentric and ecocentric perspectives, recognizing that each assigns moral importance differently and may produce different management priorities.
Evaluates trade-offs between present economic development and future environmental quality, including uncertainty and potentially irreversible harm.
Develops an integrated decision framework combining distributional justice, procedural participation, ecological limits and transparent ethical reasoning.
Explains conditions for fairer decisions such as early participation, accessible information, representation of vulnerable groups, long-term monitoring and mechanisms for compensation or remedy.
Recognizes that ethical disagreement cannot always be eliminated, so legitimate processes and explicit justification are important when values conflict.
Reaches a clear, justified judgement about how environmental justice and ethical frameworks should influence decisions across communities and generations.
markschemeJa: environmental justiceをenvironmental benefit/burdenのfair distributionとmeaningful participationを含む概念として正確に説明する。
intergenerational justiceを正確に説明し、future generationが受けるenvironmental consequenceへのobligationを認識する。
utilitarianism、rights-based ethics、deontology、anthropocentrism、biocentrism、ecocentrismなど少なくとも2つのethical framework/positionを正確に区別する。
intrinsic value、instrumental value、moral standing、stewardship、moral responsibility、ethical dilemmaなどを正確に使う。
mine、landfill、industrial facility、transport corridor、dam、protected area等の具体的decisionへenvironmental-justice reasoningを適用する。
同じdecisionへ少なくとも1つのethical frameworkを適用し、異なるconclusion/priorityを導き得ることを示す。
resource depletion、pollution、climate risk、long-lived environmental damageへintergenerational reasoningを適用する。
実例または明確なhypothetical exampleでenvironmental benefit/burdenがincome group、location、generation間で不均等に分布し得ると示す。
aggregate benefitを最大化するpolicyでもcostがvulnerable groupへ集中すればenvironmental injusticeになり得ることを分析する。
rights-based/deontological reasoningはcost-benefit analysisがnet benefitを示してもactionへlimitを置き得ることを分析する。
biocentric/ecocentric reasoningがdirect human welfareを越えてorganism、species、ecosystem integrityへmoral concernを広げることを説明する。
participation、recognition、decision-making accessがlegitimacy、trust、distributional outcomeへ影響することを説明する。
utilitarian/consequentialist approachのtotal benefit/harm比較の強みとminorityをaggregate gainのため犠牲にするriskを評価する。
rights-based approachのserious harmからの保護という強みとcompeting rights/practical constraintを評価する。
anthropocentric、biocentric、ecocentric perspectiveはmoral importanceの置き方が異なりmanagement priorityも変わることを評価する。
present economic developmentとfuture environmental qualityのtrade-offをuncertainty・irreversible harmも含め評価する。
distributional justice、procedural participation、ecological limit、transparent ethical reasoningを組み合わせたintegrated decision frameworkを構築する。
early participation、accessible information、vulnerable group representation、long-term monitoring、compensation/remedy mechanismなどfairer decisionの条件を説明する。
ethical disagreementは常に解消できないためvalue conflict時にはlegitimate processとexplicit justificationが重要と認識する。
communityとgenerationをまたぐdecisionでenvironmental justiceとethical frameworkをどう反映すべきか明確で根拠あるjudgementを示す。
modelAnswer: Environmental decisions should not be judged only by total economic benefits because both the distribution of impacts and the moral principles used matter. A new mine or waste facility may create jobs and public revenue while concentrating pollution, noise or health risks in one low-income community. Environmental justice therefore requires attention to who gains, who bears costs and whether affected people have meaningful participation. Utilitarianism may support a project if overall benefits exceed harms, but rights-based ethics may reject serious involuntary harm even when net benefits are positive. Ecocentric ethics can also give intrinsic value to ecosystems that a purely anthropocentric calculation might overlook. Intergenerational justice adds another dimension because resource depletion and persistent pollution can transfer costs to people who had no role in the original decision. Overall, good decisions should combine evidence about consequences with rights, ecological limits and fair procedures. Ethical disagreement will remain, but early participation, transparent reasoning and protection of vulnerable groups can make outcomes more legitimate and just.
modelAnswerJa: environmental decisionはtotal economic benefitだけで判断すべきではなく、impactのdistributionと使うmoral principleの両方が重要です。例えばnew mineやwaste facilityはjobやpublic revenueを生む一方、pollutionやhealth riskを特定のlow-income communityへ集中させる可能性があります。environmental justiceでは誰がbenefitを得て誰がcostを負うか、affected peopleがmeaningful participationを持つかを考える必要があります。utilitarianismはoverall benefitがharmを上回ればprojectを支持し得ますが、rights-based ethicsはnet benefitがあってもserious involuntary harmを拒否する場合があります。ecocentric ethicsはecosystemそのもののintrinsic valueを重視します。さらにintergenerational justiceではresource depletionやpersistent pollutionをfuture generationへ転嫁しないことが重要です。したがってconsequence、rights、ecological limit、fair procedureを統合し、early participation、transparent reasoning、vulnerable group protectionを備えるdecision processが最も適切です。

subject: ESS HL
question: Evaluate strategies for increasing food security while maintaining soil fertility and reducing water pollution and biodiversity loss in agricultural systems.

rubricGroups.title: Analysis / systems / HL-lens connections
rubricGroups.titleJa: 分析・システム・HL lensとの接続

rubricGroups.title: Evaluation / perspectives / trade-offs
rubricGroups.titleJa: 評価・視点・トレードオフ

markscheme: Accurately explains food security and distinguishes it from simply maximizing short-term agricultural yield.
Accurately explains soil fertility and recognizes the roles of soil organic matter, nutrient availability, structure and biological activity.
Accurately explains how agricultural inputs and land management can contribute to soil degradation, water pollution or biodiversity loss.
Uses relevant terminology such as sustainable agriculture, crop rotation, agroforestry, fertilizer, pesticide, erosion, salinization or ecosystem services accurately.
Applies at least one soil-conservation strategy, such as cover crops, reduced tillage, contour farming, terracing, organic amendments or erosion-control measures.
Applies at least one nutrient-management strategy, such as precision fertilizer application, nutrient budgeting, buffer strips or improved manure management.
Applies at least one biodiversity-supporting strategy, such as crop rotation, polyculture, agroforestry, integrated pest management or habitat retention.
Uses a relevant real or clearly hypothetical agricultural example to show how food-security strategies depend on climate, soils, farm size, markets and local livelihoods.
Analyses how maintaining soil organic matter and structure can improve nutrient retention, infiltration, water-holding capacity and long-term productivity.
Analyses how excess nitrogen or phosphorus can move from farmland into water systems and contribute to eutrophication and oxygen depletion.
Analyses how monoculture, pesticide dependence or habitat removal can simplify agroecosystems and reduce functional biodiversity and resilience.
Explains how feedbacks among soil condition, yields, farmer income and management choices can either reinforce degradation or support long-term recovery.
Evaluates high-input intensification by considering yield benefits alongside fertilizer dependence, pollution, soil degradation, energy use and vulnerability to input prices.
Evaluates low-input, organic or agroecological approaches by considering soil and biodiversity benefits alongside land requirements, labour, transition costs and possible yield gaps.
Evaluates technological approaches such as precision agriculture or improved crop varieties while recognizing affordability, access, rebound effects and context dependence.
Evaluates equity and food-access issues, recognizing that greater production does not automatically ensure affordable, nutritious food for vulnerable populations.
Develops an integrated strategy combining soil conservation, efficient nutrient use, biodiversity protection and measures that improve access to food rather than relying on one farming method.
Explains conditions for success such as extension services, secure land tenure, farmer knowledge, monitoring, incentives, market access and policies that reduce damaging externalities.
Recognizes that the most sustainable strategy depends on local climate, soil type, water availability, socioeconomic conditions and the scale of production.
Reaches a clear, justified judgement about which combination of agricultural strategies can improve food security while protecting soils, water and biodiversity.
markschemeJa: food securityを正確に説明し、単にshort-term agricultural yieldを最大化することとは区別する。
soil fertilityを正確に説明し、soil organic matter、nutrient availability、structure、biological activityの役割を認識する。
agricultural inputとland managementがsoil degradation、water pollution、biodiversity lossへつながる仕組みを正確に説明する。
sustainable agriculture、crop rotation、agroforestry、fertilizer、pesticide、erosion、salinization、ecosystem servicesなどを正確に使う。
cover crop、reduced tillage、contour farming、terracing、organic amendment、erosion controlなどsoil-conservation strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
precision fertilizer application、nutrient budgeting、buffer strip、improved manure managementなどnutrient-management strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
crop rotation、polyculture、agroforestry、integrated pest management、habitat retentionなどbiodiversity-supporting strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
実例または明確なhypothetical agricultural exampleでfood-security strategyがclimate、soil、farm size、market、local livelihoodに依存すると示す。
soil organic matterとstructureの維持がnutrient retention、infiltration、water-holding capacity、long-term productivityを改善することを分析する。
過剰なnitrogen/phosphorusがfarmlandからwater systemへ移動しeutrophicationとoxygen depletionを起こし得ることを分析する。
monoculture、pesticide dependence、habitat removalがagroecosystemを単純化しfunctional biodiversityとresilienceを低下させ得ることを分析する。
soil condition、yield、farmer income、management choiceのfeedbackがdegradationを強める場合とlong-term recoveryを支える場合を説明する。
high-input intensificationをyield benefitとfertilizer dependence、pollution、soil degradation、energy use、input-price vulnerabilityの両面から評価する。
low-input、organic、agroecological approachをsoil/biodiversity benefitとland requirement、labour、transition cost、possible yield gapの両面から評価する。
precision agricultureやimproved crop variety等のtechnologyをaffordability、access、rebound effect、context dependenceも含め評価する。
production増加だけではvulnerable populationのaffordableでnutritiousなfood accessを保証しないというequity/food-access issueを評価する。
1つのfarming methodだけに頼らずsoil conservation、efficient nutrient use、biodiversity protection、food access改善を組み合わせたintegrated strategyを構築する。
extension service、secure land tenure、farmer knowledge、monitoring、incentive、market access、damaging externalityを減らすpolicyなど成功条件を説明する。
最適なstrategyはlocal climate、soil type、water availability、socioeconomic condition、production scaleに依存すると認識する。
soil・water・biodiversityを保護しながらfood securityを改善するstrategy combinationについて明確で根拠あるjudgementを示す。
modelAnswer: Food security depends on reliable access to sufficient and nutritious food, so maximizing yield in the short term is not enough if farming degrades the soils and water systems that future production depends on. Soil-conservation measures such as cover crops, reduced tillage, crop rotation and organic amendments can reduce erosion, maintain soil organic matter and improve infiltration and nutrient retention. Nutrient management is also important. Precision fertilizer application, nutrient budgeting and riparian buffer strips can maintain crop productivity while reducing nitrate and phosphate runoff that can cause eutrophication. Biodiversity can be supported through polyculture, agroforestry, integrated pest management and retention of non-crop habitat, which can improve pollination, pest control and resilience. High-input intensification may produce high yields on limited land, but it can increase dependence on fertilizers, pesticides, energy and purchased inputs. Organic or agroecological systems may reduce some externalities but can require more labour or land and may have lower yields during transition. Technology such as precision agriculture can improve efficiency, although access and cost may exclude small farmers. Overall, the strongest strategy is context specific and combines soil conservation, efficient nutrient use, biodiversity protection and social measures that improve access to food. Food security is most durable when policy supports farmers while protecting the natural capital on which future production depends.
modelAnswerJa: food securityは十分でnutritiousなfoodへ安定してアクセスできることなので、future productionを支えるsoilやwater systemを劣化させながらshort-term yieldだけを最大化しても持続的ではありません。cover crop、reduced tillage、crop rotation、organic amendmentはerosionを減らし、soil organic matter、infiltration、nutrient retentionを維持できます。precision fertilizer application、nutrient budgeting、riparian bufferはcrop productivityを保ちながらnitrate/phosphate runoffとeutrophicationを減らせます。polyculture、agroforestry、integrated pest management、non-crop habitat retentionはpollination、pest control、resilienceを支えます。high-input intensificationはlimited landで高yieldを得られる一方、fertilizer、pesticide、energy、purchased inputへのdependenceを高める可能性があります。organic/agroecological systemはexternalityを減らせますが、transition時のyield gap、labour、land requirementが課題です。precision agricultureも効率化に有効ですがcostとaccessの問題があります。したがってsoil conservation、efficient nutrient use、biodiversity protectionとfood accessを改善するsocial measureを地域条件に合わせて組み合わせ、future productionを支えるnatural capitalを守ることが最も持続的です。

subject: ESS HL
question: Discuss the extent to which combining climate-change mitigation and adaptation can reduce risk in rapidly growing coastal cities.

rubricGroups.title: Analysis / systems / HL-lens connections
rubricGroups.titleJa: 分析・システム・HL lensとの接続

rubricGroups.title: Evaluation / perspectives / trade-offs
rubricGroups.titleJa: 評価・視点・トレードオフ

markscheme: Accurately distinguishes climate-change mitigation from adaptation and explains why both address different components of climate risk.
Accurately explains relevant coastal climate hazards such as sea-level rise, storm surge, extreme rainfall, heat or saltwater intrusion.
Accurately explains climate resilience and recognizes the interaction of hazard, exposure and vulnerability in determining risk.
Uses relevant terminology such as greenhouse gas, net zero, managed retreat, nature-based solution, green infrastructure, adaptive capacity or climate finance accurately.
Applies at least one urban mitigation strategy, such as low-carbon electricity, energy efficiency, electrification, compact planning or public transport.
Applies at least one engineered adaptation strategy, such as sea walls, surge barriers, raised infrastructure, drainage upgrades or flood-resilient buildings.
Applies at least one nature-based or planning adaptation strategy, such as mangrove or wetland restoration, green infrastructure, zoning or managed retreat.
Uses a relevant real or clearly hypothetical coastal-city example to show how strategy choice depends on hazard level, density, income, governance and available finance.
Analyses how mitigation reduces future climate forcing while adaptation mainly reduces vulnerability or exposure to impacts that cannot be avoided immediately.
Analyses how rapid urban growth can increase exposure when housing and infrastructure expand into flood-prone or heat-prone areas.
Explains how nature-based solutions can provide multiple benefits such as flood attenuation, cooling, biodiversity, recreation or carbon storage while having spatial and ecological limits.
Analyses how urban systems create feedbacks among transport, land use, energy demand, emissions, housing location and vulnerability.
Evaluates hard coastal defences by considering protection benefits alongside cost, maintenance, residual risk, ecosystem impacts and possible transfer of erosion or flooding.
Evaluates managed retreat or land-use restrictions by considering long-term risk reduction alongside property rights, livelihoods, cultural attachment, compensation and political feasibility.
Evaluates urban mitigation measures while recognizing that local emissions reductions alone cannot eliminate near-term sea-level rise or extreme-event risk.
Evaluates climate justice, recognizing that low-income or informal-settlement residents may face higher exposure and have less capacity to adapt despite contributing less to emissions.
Develops an integrated strategy combining emissions reduction, resilient infrastructure, ecosystem-based adaptation and land-use planning rather than relying on a single defence.
Explains conditions for success such as long-term finance, risk mapping, early-warning systems, building standards, public participation, maintenance and coordination across agencies.
Recognizes uncertainty in future climate hazards and urban growth, so flexible pathways and adaptive management may be preferable to one irreversible plan.
Reaches a clear, justified judgement about the extent to which combined mitigation and adaptation can reduce climate risk in rapidly growing coastal cities.
markschemeJa: climate-change mitigationとadaptationを正確に区別し、両者がclimate riskの異なる要素へ対応することを説明する。
sea-level rise、storm surge、extreme rainfall、heat、saltwater intrusionなどrelevant coastal climate hazardを正確に説明する。
climate resilienceを正確に説明し、riskがhazard、exposure、vulnerabilityの相互作用で決まると認識する。
greenhouse gas、net zero、managed retreat、nature-based solution、green infrastructure、adaptive capacity、climate financeなどを正確に使う。
low-carbon electricity、energy efficiency、electrification、compact planning、public transportなどurban mitigation strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
sea wall、surge barrier、raised infrastructure、drainage upgrade、flood-resilient buildingなどengineered adaptation strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
mangrove/wetland restoration、green infrastructure、zoning、managed retreatなどnature-based/planning adaptation strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
実例または明確なhypothetical coastal-city exampleでstrategy choiceがhazard level、density、income、governance、financeに依存すると示す。
mitigationはfuture climate forcingを減らし、adaptationは主に直ちに避けられないimpactへのvulnerability/exposureを減らすことを分析する。
rapid urban growthでhousing/infrastructureがflood-prone・heat-prone areaへ広がるとexposureが増えることを分析する。
nature-based solutionがflood attenuation、cooling、biodiversity、recreation、carbon storage等のmultiple benefitを持つ一方、space/ecological limitもあると説明する。
transport、land use、energy demand、emission、housing location、vulnerabilityの間にurban-system feedbackがあることを分析する。
hard coastal defenceをprotection benefitとcost、maintenance、residual risk、ecosystem impact、erosion/flooding transferの両面から評価する。
managed retreat/land-use restrictionをlong-term risk reductionとproperty right、livelihood、cultural attachment、compensation、political feasibilityの両面から評価する。
urban mitigation measureを評価し、local emission reductionだけではnear-term sea-level riseやextreme-event riskをなくせないと認識する。
low-income/informal-settlement residentはemissionへのcontributionが小さくてもexposureが高くadaptive capacityが低い場合があるというclimate justiceを評価する。
single defenceだけに頼らずemission reduction、resilient infrastructure、ecosystem-based adaptation、land-use planningを組み合わせたintegrated strategyを構築する。
long-term finance、risk mapping、early-warning system、building standard、public participation、maintenance、agency coordinationなど成功条件を説明する。
future climate hazardとurban growthにはuncertaintyがあるため、1つのirreversible planよりflexible pathwayとadaptive managementが有効な場合を認識する。
mitigationとadaptationの組み合わせがrapidly growing coastal cityのclimate riskをどの程度減らせるか明確で根拠あるjudgementを示す。
modelAnswer: Rapidly growing coastal cities need both mitigation and adaptation because they face immediate climate hazards while also contributing to future emissions. Mitigation measures such as low-carbon electricity, efficient buildings, public transport and compact development can reduce greenhouse-gas emissions and limit long-term warming. However, they cannot prevent all near-term sea-level rise, storm surges or extreme rainfall, so adaptation is essential. Engineered measures such as drainage upgrades, flood barriers and raised infrastructure can protect dense areas, while mangrove and wetland restoration can reduce wave energy and provide biodiversity, recreation and carbon-storage benefits. Land-use zoning and, in the highest-risk locations, managed retreat can reduce future exposure. Each option has limits: hard defences are costly and can transfer erosion or create false security; nature-based solutions need space and suitable ecological conditions; retreat can disrupt livelihoods and face strong political resistance. Climate justice is also important because low-income and informal communities often face the highest exposure but have the least adaptive capacity. Overall, combining mitigation and adaptation can reduce risk substantially, but not eliminate it. The most resilient approach uses flexible pathways: cut emissions, prevent new development in high-risk areas, protect critical infrastructure, restore coastal ecosystems and revise plans as hazards and urban growth change.
modelAnswerJa: rapidly growing coastal cityでは現在のclimate hazardへ対応しながらfuture emissionも減らす必要があるため、mitigationとadaptationの両方が必要です。low-carbon electricity、efficient building、public transport、compact developmentはGHG emissionを下げlong-term warmingを抑えますが、near-term sea-level rise、storm surge、extreme rainfallを完全には防げません。そのためdrainage upgrade、flood barrier、raised infrastructureなどengineered adaptationと、mangrove/wetland restorationなどnature-based solutionが必要です。zoningやhigh-risk areaでのmanaged retreatはfuture exposureを減らせます。ただしhard defenceは高コストでerosion transferやfalse securityを生む場合があり、nature-based solutionにはspace/ecological conditionが必要で、retreatはlivelihoodやcommunityを損なう可能性があります。さらにlow-income/informal communityほどexposureが高くadaptive capacityが低いclimate justiceの問題があります。したがってemission reduction、high-risk areaへのnew development抑制、critical infrastructure protection、coastal ecosystem restorationを組み合わせ、hazardとurban growthの変化に応じてplanを更新するflexible pathwayが最もresilientです。

subject: ESS HL
question: Evaluate the extent to which protecting intact ecosystems is more effective than restoring degraded ecosystems for conserving biodiversity and ecosystem services.

rubricGroups.title: Analysis / systems / HL-lens connections

markscheme: Accurately explains biodiversity at genetic, species and ecosystem levels and links biodiversity to ecosystem function or resilience.
Accurately distinguishes protection or prevention of degradation from ecological restoration or regeneration after degradation has occurred.
Accurately explains ecosystem services and recognizes that intact ecosystems can provide regulating, provisioning, cultural and supporting functions.
Uses relevant terminology such as habitat fragmentation, protected area, ecological connectivity, restoration ecology, resilience, threshold or reference ecosystem accurately.
Applies at least one protection strategy, such as protected areas, land-use regulation, habitat corridors, indigenous/community conservation or prevention of invasive-species introduction.
Applies at least one restoration strategy, such as reforestation, wetland restoration, invasive-species removal, rewilding, assisted regeneration or habitat reconnection.
Applies monitoring or adaptive management to assess biodiversity recovery, ecosystem function or changing threats over time.
Uses a relevant real or clearly hypothetical ecosystem example to compare the feasibility and outcomes of protection and restoration.
Analyses how intact ecosystems can retain complex species interactions, genetic diversity, soils, hydrology and ecological processes that may be difficult to recreate after degradation.
Analyses how fragmentation and edge effects can reduce population viability and connectivity even where some habitat remains protected.
Explains how restoration can improve habitat area, connectivity and ecosystem services, potentially creating positive feedbacks that support further recovery.
Analyses ecological thresholds, hysteresis or legacy effects to explain why a restored ecosystem may not return fully to its previous state.
Evaluates protection by considering high preventive value alongside opportunity costs, enforcement needs, conflicts over access and the risk of paper parks.
Evaluates restoration by considering biodiversity and ecosystem-service gains alongside cost, time lags, uncertainty, species loss and the difficulty of recreating complex ecological interactions.
Evaluates whether active restoration or passive regeneration is more appropriate under different levels of degradation and different ecological conditions.
Evaluates social and governance dimensions, including local livelihoods, indigenous rights, community participation, land tenure and the distribution of conservation costs and benefits.
Develops an integrated conservation strategy that prioritizes preventing irreversible loss while using restoration to reconnect and recover already degraded landscapes.
Explains conditions for success such as adequate area, connectivity, long-term funding, threat removal, appropriate reference conditions, monitoring and adaptive management.
Recognizes that climate change and shifting species distributions can make historical ecosystem conditions an imperfect restoration target.
Reaches a clear, justified judgement about the circumstances in which protection or restoration should receive greater priority for conserving biodiversity and ecosystem services.
markschemeJa: biodiversityをgenetic・species・ecosystem levelで正確に説明し、ecosystem function/resilienceと関連づける。
protection/prevention of degradationと、degradation後に行うecological restoration/regenerationを正確に区別する。
ecosystem servicesを正確に説明し、intact ecosystemがregulating、provisioning、cultural、supporting functionを提供し得ると認識する。
habitat fragmentation、protected area、ecological connectivity、restoration ecology、resilience、threshold、reference ecosystemなどを正確に使う。
protected area、land-use regulation、habitat corridor、indigenous/community conservation、invasive-species introduction preventionなどprotection strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
reforestation、wetland restoration、invasive-species removal、rewilding、assisted regeneration、habitat reconnectionなどrestoration strategyを少なくとも1つ適用する。
biodiversity recovery、ecosystem function、changing threatを時間的に評価するmonitoring/adaptive managementを適用する。
実例または明確なhypothetical ecosystem exampleでprotectionとrestorationのfeasibility/outcomeを比較する。
intact ecosystemではcomplex species interaction、genetic diversity、soil、hydrology、ecological processが維持され、degradation後には再現が難しいことを分析する。
一部habitatが保護されてもfragmentationとedge effectがpopulation viabilityやconnectivityを低下させ得ることを分析する。
restorationがhabitat area、connectivity、ecosystem servicesを改善し、further recoveryを支えるpositive feedbackを生み得ることを説明する。
ecological threshold、hysteresis、legacy effectによりrestored ecosystemがprevious stateへ完全に戻らない場合を分析する。
protectionをhigh preventive valueとopportunity cost、enforcement need、access conflict、paper park riskの両面から評価する。
restorationをbiodiversity/ecosystem-service gainとcost、time lag、uncertainty、species loss、complex interaction再現のdifficultyの両面から評価する。
degradation levelやecological conditionによってactive restorationとpassive regenerationのどちらが適切か評価する。
local livelihood、indigenous right、community participation、land tenure、conservation cost/benefitのdistributionなどsocial/governance dimensionを評価する。
irreversible lossのpreventionを優先しつつdegraded landscapeをreconnect/recoverするrestorationも使うintegrated conservation strategyを構築する。
adequate area、connectivity、long-term funding、threat removal、appropriate reference condition、monitoring、adaptive managementなど成功条件を説明する。
climate changeとspecies distribution shiftによりhistorical ecosystem conditionが必ずしも完全なrestoration targetにならないと認識する。
biodiversity/ecosystem services保全のため、どの条件でprotectionまたはrestorationを優先すべきか明確で根拠あるjudgementを示す。
modelAnswer: Protecting intact ecosystems is usually more effective for preventing irreversible biodiversity loss because existing communities retain complex species interactions, genetic diversity, soils, hydrology and ecological processes that can be extremely difficult to rebuild. Protected areas, habitat corridors and land-use controls can therefore preserve ecosystem services at lower ecological risk than allowing degradation and attempting repair later. However, protection alone is insufficient because many landscapes are already fragmented or degraded. Restoration can expand habitat, reconnect populations and recover services such as water regulation, carbon storage and erosion control. Reforestation, wetland restoration, invasive-species removal and assisted regeneration can be effective where the main pressures have been removed. Restoration also has important limits: recovery may take decades, extinct local populations cannot always be replaced, and thresholds or legacy effects may prevent a return to the previous ecosystem state. Protected areas can also fail if they lack enforcement or exclude local communities from benefits and decision-making. Overall, prevention should generally receive first priority where intact ecosystems and irreplaceable biodiversity remain, because avoided damage is more reliable than reconstruction. Restoration is nevertheless essential for already degraded systems and for reconnecting protected areas. The strongest conservation strategy therefore combines strict protection of high-value intact habitat with targeted, monitored restoration across the surrounding landscape.
modelAnswerJa: intact ecosystemのprotectionは、complex species interaction、genetic diversity、soil、hydrology、ecological processをそのまま維持できるため、irreversible biodiversity lossを防ぐ方法として一般に最も確実です。protected area、habitat corridor、land-use controlはdegradation後にrepairするよりecological riskを低くできます。しかし多くのlandscapeはすでにfragmented/degradedなのでprotectionだけでは不十分です。reforestation、wetland restoration、invasive-species removal、assisted regenerationはhabitat areaとconnectivityを増やし、water regulation、carbon storage、erosion control等のecosystem serviceを回復できます。ただしrecoveryにはdecadesかかる場合があり、local extinction、ecological threshold、legacy effectによってprevious stateへ完全には戻れないことがあります。またprotected areaもenforcement不足やlocal community排除があれば失敗します。したがってintact habitatとirreplaceable biodiversityが残る場所ではpreventionを第一優先とし、すでにdegradedな場所ではtargeted restorationを行い、protected area同士をlandscape scaleでつなぐ組み合わせが最も有効です。
